stemMd: A farmer in Puglia sows clover to raise the nitrogen content of a field. Bacteria living in nodules on the roots of the clover convert nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia that the plant can use. What is this process called?
explanationMd:
The key phrase in the question is "nitrogen gas from the air" turned into ammonia. Only nitrogen fixation begins with atmospheric $N_{2}$. Clover and other legumes host *Rhizobium* bacteria in root nodules, which fix nitrogen and supply the plant with ammonia.

The other steps of the nitrogen cycle can be told apart by what they start from and end with: nitrification (ammonium to nitrite and nitrate), denitrification (nitrate to nitrogen gas), ammonification (organic nitrogen to ammonium) and assimilation (ammonium or nitrate taken up and built into plant tissue).

distractorRationale.a: Nitrification is the oxidation of ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate by soil bacteria. It starts from ammonium, not nitrogen gas.
distractorRationale.c: Denitrification does the reverse job in the cycle: bacteria convert nitrate back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.
distractorRationale.b: Ammonification is the release of ammonium from dead organic matter by decomposers. It recycles nitrogen already in the soil and does not take it from the air.
distractorRationale.e: Assimilation is the uptake of ammonium or nitrate by plant roots. It moves nitrogen into the plant and does not bring nitrogen gas into the soil.

accessibilityText: A short text question with no figure. A farmer sows clover to raise the nitrogen in a field. Bacteria in root nodules of clover convert nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia, and the question asks the name of this process. The five choices are steps of the nitrogen cycle: nitrification, ammonification, denitrification, nitrogen fixation and assimilation.

provenance.notes: Original item on the nitrogen cycle. Each distractor is another named step of the cycle, so the item tests whether the learner can tell the steps apart by their starting material.

independentSolve.workingNotes: Rhizobium in legume root nodules convert N2 to NH3, which is biological nitrogen fixation. Nitrification is NH4+ to NO3-, ammonification is organic N to NH4+, and denitrification is NO3- to N2. Assimilation is the plant incorporating the ammonia, not the bacteria converting N2, so it does not describe the process in the stem. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tolcf-bio-run19) reached the same answer: Rhizobium in the root nodules reduces N2 to NH3, which is nitrogen fixation. Nitrification oxidises NH4+ to NO3-. Ammonification releases NH4+ from organic matter. Denitrification turns NO3- into N2. Assimilation is the plant taking up the fixed N, which is not the conversion the stem describes.]
